e.etymology: Often a pet form of Tolliver or Tolbert, surnames used as given names in the South.
Given in 1918 and the years after in honor of General John J. Pershing, commander of American forces in World War I. His family name was Americanized from a German surname.

assoc.t: General John J. Pershing of World War I

e.etymology: An American elaboration of Sydney or Sidney with the -ell ending, used mostly in the 1920s and 1930s.

e.note: Contains the word girth, which invites teasing.

e.etymology: A variant of Odis and Otis, from an English surname based on the Germanic name Odo or Otto, wealth.
Shares its root with iris and iridescent: Greek iris, rainbow. In the United States it was used mainly by Spanish-speaking families in the 1990s.
A short form of Carlota or Charlotte, like Lotta and Lottie.
A surname from Astbury in Cheshire, Old English for the eastern fort. American Methodists gave it to sons in honor of Francis Asbury, one of their first two bishops.

assoc.t: Asbury Park, the New Jersey shore town

e.etymology: From Capitola Black, the daring heroine of E. D. E. N. Southworth's The Hidden Hand, a hit serial novel of 1859. The California beach town of Capitola is said to be named for her as well.
From Ciji Dunne, the singer played by Lisa Hartman on the prime-time soap Knots Landing in 1982 and 1983. The name's 1983 peak follows the character.
A spelling of Mattie, the pet form of Matilda and Martha.
A short form of Augusta, the feminine of Augustus, Latin for venerable or majestic, a title of Roman empresses.
The double name Shirley Ann written as one word. Shirley is an English place name, bright clearing, and Ann goes back to Hebrew Hannah, grace.
A spelling of Della, a short form of Adela and Adelaide, from Germanic adal, noble. The final r records a Southern way of saying the name.
An English surname from two Old English names, Sigeweard, victory guardian, and Saeweard, sea guardian.

assoc.t: William Seward, who bought Alaska for the US in 1867

e.etymology: The family word used as a given name, a Southern custom in which the household nickname Sister sometimes went onto the record.
e.note: Reads as the family word or a nun's title, so people may not take it for a name.

e.etymology: A short form of Harvey, from the Breton name Haerviu, battle worthy, which Bretons brought to England with the Norman Conquest.
The Finnish word for hope, used as a boys' name since the 19th century. Finnish immigrants brought it to Michigan and Minnesota, where Toivo and Eino became the stock pair in local jokes.
A spelling of the surname Pinckney, of Norman origin. Southern families gave it in honor of the Pinckneys of South Carolina, statesmen of the founding era.
A grayling is a silvery freshwater fish of the salmon family; Grayling is also an English surname and a town in Michigan.
An old American spelling that follows the spoken short form of Elijah, Hebrew Eliyahu, my God is Yahweh, the name of the Old Testament prophet.
An Americanized form of Dmytro, the Ukrainian form of Demetrius, follower of the goddess Demeter. Ukrainian and Rusyn immigrant families used it in the early 1900s.

assoc.t: metro, the word for a subway or a city area

e.etymology: An English surname from the town of Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, open land by the River Maun.

A spelling of Ella that records the Southern habit of sounding a final -a as -er. Ella came to England with the Normans, from Germanic alia, other, and later served as a short form of Eleanor and Ellen.
Identical to the Latin and Spanish word pluma, feather.
A short form of Alabama, which was itself given to Southern girls in the 19th century.

assoc.t: Bama, nickname for Alabama and its Crimson Tide

e.etymology: Known almost entirely through heavyweight champion Ezzard Charles, who was named for the doctor who delivered him, W. P. Ezzard. Boys were given the name during his title reign.
namesakes: Ezzard Charles (world heavyweight boxing champion, 1949 to 1951)
